sections.heading: Seeing your love in everything you did for me
sections.text: Lord Jesus, help me see how far your love has gone for me. Let me read your heart in your coming as a baby, in your anguish in Gethsemane, in your suffering on the cross, in your empty tomb, and in your ongoing work for me at the Father’s side. Do not let these truths stay distant or familiar. Let them show me, again and again, that you have loved me all the way.
theological_themes: Christ's incarnate humility, suffering, death, resurrection, and intercession reveal the depth and constancy of his love for sinners.

scripture_references.connection: John frames Jesus' final suffering as the fullest expression of his love for his own. This supports the prayer's desire to see Christ's heart revealed through the whole saving work that leads to the cross.

Hebrews presents the risen Christ as continually interceding for those who come to God through him. This grounds the prayer's confidence that Jesus' love did not end at the cross or the tomb but continues in heaven.

sections.heading: Standing firm because you are for me
sections.text: Because this is true, give me courage. When the enemy accuses me, help me answer with what you have done. When temptation comes, help me refuse it. When lies are dressed up as wisdom, help me see through them. When the world tries to win my heart, help me turn away from it. Make me brave for what is true, not because I am strong in myself, but because I belong to you.
theological_themes: Christ's completed work gives the believer courage against accusation, temptation, deception, worldliness, and compromise.

scripture_references.connection: Paul answers every accusation against God's people by pointing to Christ's death, resurrection, exaltation, and intercession. That is the same logic behind the prayer's boldness against the adversary.
James calls believers to submit to God and resist the devil. The prayer asks for that resistance to be rooted not in self-confidence but in allegiance to Christ.

sections.heading: Knowing who you are and who I am before you
sections.text:
Deepen my sense of how holy and personal my relationship with you is. You are the Bridegroom who has given himself for your people. You are equal with the Father, worthy of all honor. You are the Friend of sinners, near to people who have nothing to offer you but need.

When I look at you, I see glory; when I look honestly at myself, I see how low and unworthy I am. You are majestic, and I am small. You are beautiful, and sin has twisted me. You are pure, and I am stained. You are righteous, and I am full of wrong. Keep me from pretending otherwise. Let the truth about me make the truth about you even more precious.
theological_themes: Christ is exalted and divine, yet he draws near to sinners in covenant love; honest self-knowledge magnifies grace rather than producing despair.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes Christ as the husband who loved the church and gave himself up to make her holy. This supports the Bridegroom imagery and the prayer's longing to be clothed in what Christ gives.
This passage holds together Christ's equality with God and his humble self-giving. It illuminates the prayer's worship of Christ's majesty alongside his nearness to sinners.
Jesus was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, a title meant as criticism but revealing his merciful mission. The prayer receives that truth with gratitude and humility.

sections.heading: Loving you because you loved me first
sections.text: You have loved me with a love that did not begin when I improved and will not end when I fail. Teach me to love you with the love I have received from you. You gave yourself for me; teach me to give myself back to you. You died for me; teach me to live for you—in my time, my thoughts, my desires, my choices, and every beat of my heart.
theological_themes: The believer's love, surrender, and obedience are a response to Christ's prior, unchanging, self-giving love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks personally of the Son of God loving him and giving himself for him, and of the believer's life now being lived by faith in Christ. This closely supports the prayer's movement from Christ's self-giving to a life given back to him.
John grounds the believer's love in God's prior love. The prayer asks to love Christ not as an achievement but as a response to being loved first.

sections.heading: Walking with you instead of flirting with the world
sections.text: Keep me from playing around with the world’s promises as if they were harmless. Do not let me be charmed by what pulls me away from you. Keep me close to your side. Train me to recognize your voice and follow it. Dress my life with your grace, and let the righteousness you give be what marks me most.
theological_themes: Faithfulness to Christ involves rejecting worldly allurements, listening to his voice, walking with him, and living in the righteousness and grace he provides.

scripture_references.connection: John warns believers not to love the world and its desires because they are passing away and opposed to the Father's will. This directly supports the prayer's refusal to be drawn away by worldly allurements.
Jesus describes his sheep as those who hear his voice and follow him, held securely by him. This grounds the prayer's request to stay near Christ and listen to him.

Paul rejects every rival confidence in order to gain Christ and be found in the righteousness that comes through faith. This supports the prayer's desire to be adorned not with self-made goodness but with Christ's righteousness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase 'spiritual Bridegroom' uses bridal imagery for an individual believer, though in Scripture the Bride is primarily the church corporately. The adaptation keeps the imagery but phrases it in relation to Christ giving himself for his people, while still allowing the individual to pray personally from within that covenant relationship.

The original phrase 'Jehovah’s Fellow' is a high Christological expression, likely echoing Zechariah 13:7 and Puritan usage for Christ's equality with God. Because that wording is unfamiliar today and could sound obscure, it was rendered as Christ being equal with the Father and worthy of divine honor.

The original includes strong language about the believer's 'vileness,' 'deformity,' 'filth,' and 'iniquity.' The adaptation preserves the unsparing confession of sin without importing contempt for the body or implying that creaturely smallness itself is evil.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'May I read the meltings of thy heart' was interpreted as asking to perceive Christ's loving heart through the major events of redemption: incarnation, agony, cross, resurrection, and intercession.

'Bold in this thought' was taken to mean that confidence against Satan, temptation, and the world comes specifically from Christ's saving love and present intercession, not from personal moral strength.

'Dally with the world and its allurements' was rendered as 'playing around with the world's promises' and 'flirting with the world' to preserve the original's sense of dangerous half-hearted compromise rather than merely living in ordinary earthly responsibilities.

'Be clothed with thy graces, and adorned with thy righteousness' was interpreted as both sanctifying grace evident in life and the believer's righteousness in Christ, so the adaptation avoids reducing it either to moral improvement alone or to justification language alone.
